title: Untitled
material: ink, pen and watercolour on paper
description: Artist Name: MARK TOBEY | Artwork Title: Untitled | Lot Info: (1890-1976) | Untitled signed and dated 'Tobey '58' (lower right) and further dated and inscribed 'To Ross Oct 24 1958' (lower right margin) ink, pen and watercolour on paper Image: 12 x 13.5cm (4 3/4 x 5 3/8in). Sheet: 15.9 x 14.9cm (6 1/4 x 5 7/8in). Executed in 1958
provenance: Ross Woodman Collection, US (a gift from the artist). | Private Collection, Canada (a gift from the above). | Acquired from the above by the present owner. |  |  |  | Born in 1890, Mark Tobey was one of the most influential American Abstract Expressionist artists of the 20th century.  |  | Tobey's works represent a conscious synthesis of the East and West, successfully harmonising two seemingly contradictory worlds. His extensive travels to East Asia had a lasting and transformative influence on his artistic vision. Particularly formative were his visits to Japan and China, where he explored Asian calligraphy techniques.  |  | In 1934, Tobey spent a month in a tranquil Zen Buddhist monastery in Kyoto, where he practiced meditation, studied calligraphy, and wrote poetry. This slow period deepened his spiritual understanding and affirmed his sense of belonging to both Eastern and Western cultures. During these visits, he closely studied Japanese sumi ink techniques and brushwork to understand their calligraphy practices. By 1957, under the profound influence of his experiences in the Far East, Tobey began to focus on Japanese ink painting, marking a significant evolution in his artistic journey and his penetration into the world view of the East.  |  | Tobey's deep religious beliefs and, particularly, his conversion to the Bahá'í faith in 1918 at the age of 28, infused his work with a sense of spiritual unity. Bahá'í, a religion which unites all religions, with its sense of the unity of all mankind, has guided Tobey throughout his life. His encounters with Baha'i and Zen Buddhism led him to introduce the techniques and concepts of the Orient into Western art.  |  | The present work, executed in 1958—the same year Tobey was awarded the Grand International Prize for Painting at the Venice Biennale—belongs to his acclaimed Sumi series. This body of work is widely regarded as a defining period in Tobey's oeuvre, showcasing his mature synthesis of technique, spirituality, and cross-cultural dialogue.  |  | Inscribed 'To Ross Oct 24, 1958', the work was dedicated and gifted to Tobey's close friend Ross Woodman, who would later deliver the eulogy at the artist's funeral in 1976, and subsequently gift the piece to the present owner.

title: Horse drawn sleds in a winter landscape
description: Artist Name: KINOSUKE EBIHARA | Artwork Title: Horse drawn sleds in a winter landscape | Lot Info: (1904-1970) | Horse drawn sleds in a winter landscape signed 'Ebihara' (lower right); signed 'Ebi' (on the reverse) oil on panel 19.2 x 24.2cm (7 9/16 x 9 1/2in). Painted circa 1928-1930
provenance: (Possibly) Gustave Kahn Collection, France.  | Hollywood Road Gallery, London. | Private collection, London (acquired from the above circa 1992). |  | Just as his mentor Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita before him, Kinosuke Ebihara had trained as a fine artist in Japan and subsequently made his way to France to experience the European avant-garde.  |  | After moving to Paris in 1923, Ebihara searched out the company and guidance of his countryman, gaining access to the artists and collectors of the day through the exuberant Foujita and eventually exhibiting his work at the Salon de l'Escalier. From this point on he gained greater recognition and success, leading to a dedicated exhibition of his works in New York in 1928. Ebihara continued to travel back and forth between Japan and France throughout his life, and returned to visit Foujita before his death in 1970.  |  | As one of the many émigré artists that made up the École de Paris, Ebihara was perhaps best known for his depictions of snow, typically employing the unique blue pigment seen in the present work.

description: Artist Name: ÉMILE-GUSTAVE CAVALLO-PEDUZZI | Artwork Title: Nature morte aux pommes et aux poires | Lot Info: (1851-1917) | Nature morte aux pommes et aux poires signed and dated 'Cavallo-Peduzzi 1895' (lower right) oil on canvas 45.6 x 61cm (17 15/16 x 24in). Painted in 1895
provenance: Private collection, France; their sale, La Salle des Enchères, Saint-Quentin, 27 April 2024, lot 108. | Acquired at the above sale by the present owner. | | | | This richly composed still life by Émile-Gustave Cavallo-Peduzzi, painted in 1895, is a significant departure from the more widely recognised pointillist landscapes of the artist. This painting is also a rare glimpse into the more intimate and studio-based work of the artist known for his contribution to the Neo-Impressionist movement, considering he was a founding member of the Group of Lagny alongside Maximilien Luce, Lucien Pissarro and Léo Gausson. | | Known for his luminous scenery and influenced by Seurat's Divisionist theories of colours, Cavallo-Peduzzi was also academically trained under Jean-Léon Gérôme and Eugène Froment at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, which enabled him to exhibit for the first time at the Salon des Indépendants in 1884. | | In the present work, Cavallo-Peduzzi turns his attention to the still life genre with remarkable sensitivity. At the centre of the composition is a black ceramic pitcher, placed amidst an array of pears, apples and peaches. The dark pointillistic backdrop made of crosshatched red and blue strokes, and the contrasting white draped tablecloth beneath adds a sense of weight to the scene, reminiscent of Cézanne's Nature morte aux pommes (1890) and Pot vert et bouilloire d'étain (1867-1869). | | Cavallo-Peduzzi's technical versatility and masterful handling of light and darkness exemplify his ability to shift between avant-garde innovation and classical restraint. As the artist creates tension with his muted-colour palette by playing with the tonal layering of colour evocative of 19th century Realism, he showcases his understanding of the interplay of colour and light in his best-known pointillist style and his modern sensibility. | | Still life subjects by Cavallo-Peduzzi are exceptionally rare and offer an intimate studio-based practice of an artist primarily celebrated for his en plein air landscapes, making this piece a notable rediscovery of his known body of work. Furthermore, the year 1895 places the painting at a pivotal moment of Cavallo-Peduzzi's career, as he had begun to refine his vision outside of strict divisionism and exploring more personal and reflective subjects.
